problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

| ${3}^{{J}_{2}(1)}=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |

examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Block
examples.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block $J_n(\lambda),$ we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/738039128c2eef5b848f6114c6008188456705206879411c9dab82e919bc18b5.png)

In this case, we have $f(x) = 2^{x},$ $n=4,$ and $\lambda=1.$

Since $n=4,$ we need to compute the first $4-1=3$ derivatives of $f{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={2}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={2}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & ={2}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{4}(1)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) & \frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(1) \\ 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{2}^{1} & {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} & \frac{1}{6}\cdot {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{3} \\ 0 & {2}^{1} & {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{1} & {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & {2}^{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & (\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} & \frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{3} \\ 0 & 2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & (\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ with diagonal entries ${\lambda }_{1},…,{\lambda }_{n},$ we have

$$
f(D)=[\begin{aligned}f({\lambda }_{1}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & f({\lambda }_{n})\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡D & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
